title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
description: Mechanical Properties of Solids — Class 11 Physics (NCERT): stress, strain, Hooke's law, the stress–strain curve, Young's, bulk and shear moduli, Poisson's ratio and elastic PE, with solved numericals & tests.

topics.title: Stress, Strain & Hooke's Law
topics.concept:
Push or pull on a rigid body and, strictly, no body is perfectly rigid — it changes shape or size, however slightly. When an external force acts on a body and tends to change its length, volume or shape, we call it a deforming force. The body resists this change because the molecules, pulled away from their equilibrium positions, set up internal restoring forces. The property by which a body regains its original shape and size once the deforming force is removed is called elasticity.

Stress is the internal restoring force set up per unit area of cross-section. In magnitude it equals the applied force per unit area:

  • $\text{Stress}=\frac{F}{A}$, SI unit $\text{N/m}^2$ or pascal $(\text{Pa})$; dimensional formula $[\text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]$.
  • Tensile stress — force stretches the body (longitudinal, length increases).
  • Compressive stress — force squeezes the body (longitudinal, length decreases).
  • Shear (tangential) stress — force acts parallel to a face, sliding one layer over another.
  • Hydraulic (volume) stress — a fluid presses equally from all sides, changing the volume.

Strain is the measure of deformation — the fractional change produced. Being a ratio of two like quantities, strain is a dimensionless number with no unit:

  • Longitudinal strain $=\frac{\Delta L}{L}$ (change in length / original length).
  • Volumetric strain $=\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ (change in volume / original volume).
  • Shear strain $=\frac{\Delta x}{L}=\tan\theta\approx\theta$ (relative sideways shift / height) for small angles.

Hooke's law is the foundation of this whole chapter. It states that, within the elastic limit, the stress developed in a body is directly proportional to the strain produced:

  • $\text{Stress}\propto\text{Strain}$, so $\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\text{constant}=E$, the modulus of elasticity.
  • The law only holds for small deformations — beyond the elastic limit, stress and strain are no longer proportional.

The full story is told by the stress–strain curve obtained by stretching a wire to breaking point. The straight portion from O obeys Hooke's law up to the proportional limit (A). Just beyond lies the elastic limit (B), the maximum stress from which the body still returns to its original shape. Past the yield point (C) the material deforms plastically — strain increases with little extra stress, and the deformation becomes permanent. The curve rises to the maximum ultimate tensile strength and finally reaches the fracture point (D) where the wire snaps. A large gap between the yield and fracture points means the material is ductile; a small gap means it is brittle.

examples.problem: A steel wire of cross-sectional area $2\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$ is stretched by a force of 100 N. Calculate the tensile stress in the wire.
A wire of original length 2 m is stretched so that its length increases by 1 mm. Find the longitudinal strain produced.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\text{Strain}=\frac{\Delta L}{L}$ with $\Delta L=1\ \text{mm}=1\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$ and $L=2\ \text{m}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\text{Strain}=\frac{1\times10^{-3}}{2}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\text{Strain}=5\times10^{-4}$ (no unit).

Answer: $\text{Strain}=5\times10^{-4}$ (dimensionless).

examples.problem: A force of 50 N is applied tangentially to the top face of a cube of side 0.1 m fixed at its base. Find the shear stress on the top face.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Shear stress $=\frac{F}{A}$ where $A$ is the area of the face on which the tangential force acts.
  2. Step 2: Area $A=(0.1)^2=0.01\ \text{m}^2$; substitute: $\text{Shear stress}=\frac{50}{0.01}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\text{Shear stress}=5000\ \text{N/m}^2$.

Answer: $\text{Shear stress}=5\times10^{3}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

examples.problem: The top face of a 0.5 m tall block is displaced sideways by 2 mm relative to the fixed bottom face. Find the shear strain.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Shear strain $=\frac{\Delta x}{L}$ (sideways shift / height), with $\Delta x=2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$ and $L=0.5\ \text{m}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\text{Shear strain}=\frac{2\times10^{-3}}{0.5}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\text{Shear strain}=4\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$.

Answer: $\text{Shear strain}=4\times10^{-3}$ (the angle $\theta$ in radians).

examples.problem: Within the elastic limit a wire shows a stress of $2\times10^{8}\ \text{N/m}^2$ when the strain is $1\times10^{-3}$. Find the modulus of elasticity of the wire material.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: By Hooke's law the modulus $E=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $E=\frac{2\times10^{8}}{1\times10^{-3}}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $E=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

Answer: $E=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$ (this is the order of $Y$ for steel).

examples.problem: Two wires P and Q of the same material have the same length but the radius of P is twice that of Q. If equal forces are applied to each, compare the tensile stresses in P and Q.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Stress $=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{F}{\pi r^2}$, so for equal $F$ the stress $\propto\frac{1}{r^2}$.
  2. Step 2: With $r_P=2r_Q$, $\frac{\text{Stress}_P}{\text{Stress}_Q}=\frac{r_Q^2}{r_P^2}=\frac{r_Q^2}{(2r_Q)^2}=\frac{1}{4}$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore the stress in P is one-fourth of that in Q.

Answer: $\text{Stress}_P:\text{Stress}_Q=1:4$.

recap: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area, $\text{Stress}=\frac{F}{A}$, measured in $\text{N/m}^2$ (Pa); it may be tensile, compressive, shear or hydraulic.
Strain is the fractional deformation and is dimensionless: longitudinal $\frac{\Delta L}{L}$, volumetric $\frac{\Delta V}{V}$, shear $\frac{\Delta x}{L}$.
Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, $\text{Stress}\propto\text{Strain}$, so $\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=E$ (modulus of elasticity).
On the stress–strain curve: proportional limit (Hooke's law holds), elastic limit (returns to shape), yield point (permanent set), then fracture.
A wide yield-to-fracture region means a ductile material; a narrow one means a brittle material.

quiz.q: The SI unit of stress is the same as that of:
quiz.explanation: Stress is force per unit area, $\text{N/m}^2$, the same unit as pressure (pascal).
Strain is a ratio of two like quantities (e.g. $\frac{\Delta L}{L}$), so it has no unit and no dimensions.
Stress is proportional to strain only up to the elastic (proportional) limit; beyond it the law fails.

quiz.q: When a force is applied tangentially (parallel) to a face of a body, the stress produced is:
quiz.explanation: A tangential force sliding one layer over another sets up shear (tangential) stress.

topics.title: Moduli of Elasticity
topics.concept:
Hooke's law tells us that stress divided by strain is a constant — the modulus of elasticity. Because a solid can be deformed in three distinct ways (changing length, volume or shape), there are three corresponding moduli. Each measures how stiff a material is against that particular kind of deformation: a large modulus means the material is hard to deform.

Young's modulus ($Y$) measures resistance to a change in length. It is the ratio of longitudinal (tensile or compressive) stress to longitudinal strain:

  • $Y=\frac{\text{Longitudinal stress}}{\text{Longitudinal strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}=\frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$.
  • SI unit $\text{N/m}^2$ (Pa); for steel $Y\approx2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$, larger than for copper or aluminium, so steel is stiffer.
  • The extension of a loaded wire follows $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$ — a longer or thinner wire stretches more for the same load.

Bulk modulus ($B$) measures resistance to a change in volume when a body is squeezed equally from all sides by a pressure $\Delta P$:

  • $B=\frac{\text{Volume (hydraulic) stress}}{\text{Volume strain}}=-\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$.
  • The negative sign shows the volume decreases as pressure increases, keeping $B$ positive.
  • Solids have a large bulk modulus, liquids smaller, gases the smallest — which is why gases are so easily compressed.

Compressibility ($k$) is simply the reciprocal of the bulk modulus, $k=\frac{1}{B}$. A highly compressible substance (a gas) has a small bulk modulus and a large compressibility.

Shear (rigidity) modulus ($\eta$ or $G$) measures resistance to a change in shape. It is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain:

  • $\eta=\frac{\text{Shear stress}}{\text{Shear strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\theta}=\frac{F}{A\theta}$, where $\theta$ is the angle of shear in radians.
  • Only solids possess rigidity (a non-zero shear modulus); fluids cannot sustain a shear stress at rest, so they flow.

Poisson's ratio ($\sigma$) captures a familiar fact: stretch a rubber band lengthwise and it gets thinner. The longitudinal extension is accompanied by a lateral (sideways) contraction. Poisson's ratio is defined as:

  • $\sigma=-\frac{\text{Lateral strain}}{\text{Longitudinal strain}}=\frac{\Delta d/d}{\Delta L/L}$ (taken as a positive number).
  • It is a pure number with no unit; for most metals $\sigma$ lies between about $0.2$ and $0.4$. Theoretically $\sigma$ can range from $-1$ to $+0.5$.

examples.problem: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area $1\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$ stretches by 0.4 mm under a load of 40 N. Find Young's modulus of the wire.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $Y=\frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$ with $\Delta L=0.4\ \text{mm}=4\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $Y=\frac{40\times2}{1\times10^{-6}\times4\times10^{-4}}=\frac{80}{4\times10^{-10}}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $Y=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

Answer: $Y=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

examples.problem: A load of 5 kg is attached to a wire of length 1 m and area $2\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$ with $Y=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$. Find the extension produced. (Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$ with $F=mg=5\times10=50\ \text{N}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\Delta L=\frac{50\times1}{2\times10^{-7}\times2\times10^{11}}=\frac{50}{4\times10^{4}}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\Delta L=1.25\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}=1.25\ \text{mm}$.

Answer: $\Delta L=1.25\ \text{mm}$.

examples.problem: A pressure of $2\times10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$ is applied to a liquid, reducing its volume by $0.1\%$. Find the bulk modulus of the liquid.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $B=\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$ (magnitude). Here $\frac{\Delta V}{V}=0.1\%=1\times10^{-3}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $B=\frac{2\times10^{6}}{1\times10^{-3}}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $B=2\times10^{9}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

Answer: $B=2\times10^{9}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

examples.problem: The bulk modulus of water is $2.2\times10^{9}\ \text{N/m}^2$. Find its compressibility.
A tangential force of 200 N is applied to the top face (area $0.02\ \text{m}^2$) of a block, producing a shear strain of $0.001\ \text{rad}$. Find the shear modulus of the material.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\eta=\frac{F/A}{\theta}$.
  2. Step 2: Shear stress $=\frac{200}{0.02}=1\times10^{4}\ \text{N/m}^2$; then $\eta=\frac{1\times10^{4}}{0.001}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\eta=1\times10^{7}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

Answer: $\eta=1\times10^{7}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

examples.problem: A wire of length 1 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by 1 mm. Its diameter decreases by $0.0003$ mm. Find Poisson's ratio for the material.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Longitudinal strain $=\frac{\Delta L}{L}=\frac{1\times10^{-3}}{1}=1\times10^{-3}$.
  2. Step 2: Lateral strain $=\frac{\Delta d}{d}=\frac{0.0003}{1}=3\times10^{-4}$.
  3. Step 3: $\sigma=\frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}=\frac{3\times10^{-4}}{1\times10^{-3}}=0.3$.

Answer: $\sigma=0.3$ (no unit).

recap: Young's modulus: $Y=\frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$ measures resistance to change in length; steel $Y\approx2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$.
Bulk modulus: $B=-\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$ measures resistance to change in volume; the negative sign keeps $B$ positive.
Compressibility is the reciprocal of bulk modulus, $k=\frac{1}{B}$.
Shear (rigidity) modulus: $\eta=\frac{F/A}{\theta}$ measures resistance to change in shape; only solids have rigidity.
Poisson's ratio $\sigma=-\frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}$ is a dimensionless number, about $0.2$–$0.4$ for most metals.

quiz.q: Young's modulus is the ratio of:
The bulk modulus relates to a change in:
quiz.explanation: $B=-\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$ measures resistance to a change in volume under uniform pressure.

quiz.q: Which type of modulus is possessed only by solids and not by fluids at rest?
quiz.explanation: Fluids cannot sustain a shear stress at rest, so only solids have a non-zero shear modulus.
It is the ratio of two strains, hence dimensionless; for metals it is roughly $0.2$–$0.4$.

topics.title: Elastic Behaviour & Applications
topics.concept:
When you stretch a wire you do work against the internal restoring forces, and that work is stored inside the deformed body as elastic potential energy. Release the load and the energy is given back as the body springs to its original shape — exactly what makes a catapult, a bow or a trampoline work.

For a wire stretched by an amount $\Delta L$, the restoring force grows from $0$ to its final value $F$, so the average force is $\frac{F}{2}$. The work done — and hence the energy stored — is:

  • $U=\frac{1}{2}\times F\times\Delta L=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{Stress}\times\text{Strain}\times\text{Volume}$.
  • The elastic energy per unit volume (energy density) is $u=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{Stress}\times\text{Strain}=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{(\text{Stress})^2}{Y}$.
  • This corresponds to the area under the stress–strain graph within the elastic region.

Real materials are not perfectly elastic. Two effects matter in engineering:

  • Elastic after-effect: some materials do not return to their original shape instantly when the load is removed — there is a small time delay before full recovery. Quartz and phosphor-bronze show almost no after-effect, which is why they are used in sensitive instruments.
  • Elastic fatigue: a material subjected to repeated cycles of stress gradually becomes weaker and may break at a stress far below its normal breaking value. This is why bridges, aircraft parts and railway tracks are inspected and replaced before failure, and why a wire bent back and forth many times eventually snaps.

Applications of elasticity turn these ideas into safe, economical design:

  • Cables and ropes: the maximum safe load on a rope is fixed by the breaking stress of its material. To lift heavy loads, engineers use a rope made of many thin strands twisted together (a stranded rope) rather than one thick wire, since this gives flexibility with the required cross-sectional area, and they apply a generous factor of safety.
  • Beams in bridges and buildings: a horizontal beam supported at its ends sags by a depression $\delta=\frac{W L^3}{4 b d^3 Y}$ under a central load $W$. The depression falls sharply (as $\frac{1}{d^3}$) when the depth $d$ is increased, so beams are made deep rather than wide, and an I-shaped (girder) cross-section puts material where it resists bending best while saving weight.
  • Cantilevers: a beam fixed at one end and free at the other (a balcony, a diving board) bends most at its free end; its load capacity is again governed by Young's modulus and the depth of the section.
  • Pillars and columns: the maximum height of a column is limited by the compressive strength of its material, which is why the legs of furniture and supporting columns have a large cross-section.

The recurring lesson is that a material with a high Young's modulus and a high elastic limit, used in a well-chosen shape, lets engineers build structures that are both strong and light.

examples.problem: A wire is stretched by a force of 100 N producing an extension of 2 mm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the wire.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $U=\frac{1}{2}\times F\times\Delta L$ with $\Delta L=2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $U=\frac{1}{2}\times100\times2\times10^{-3}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $U=0.1\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $U=0.1\ \text{J}$.

examples.problem: A wire of volume $1\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^3$ is subjected to a stress of $4\times10^{7}\ \text{N/m}^2$ producing a strain of $2\times10^{-4}$. Find the elastic potential energy stored.
Find the elastic energy density (energy per unit volume) in a material where the stress is $2\times10^{8}\ \text{N/m}^2$ and $Y=2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$.
A steel cable can withstand a maximum (breaking) stress of $3\times10^{8}\ \text{N/m}^2$. What is the maximum load it can support if its cross-sectional area is $2\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Maximum load $F=\text{Breaking stress}\times A$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $F=3\times10^{8}\times2\times10^{-4}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $F=6\times10^{4}\ \text{N}$.

Answer: $F=6\times10^{4}\ \text{N}$ (engineers would apply a factor of safety and rate it lower).

examples.problem: A beam supported at its two ends sags by $\delta$ under a central load. If the depth $d$ of the beam is doubled (all else fixed), by what factor does the sag change? Use $\delta=\frac{W L^3}{4 b d^3 Y}$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: From the formula, $\delta\propto\frac{1}{d^3}$ when $W$, $L$, $b$ and $Y$ are fixed.
  2. Step 2: Doubling $d$: $\delta'\propto\frac{1}{(2d)^3}=\frac{1}{8d^3}$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $\delta'=\frac{\delta}{8}$.

Answer: The sag reduces to one-eighth — which is why beams are made deep rather than wide.

examples.problem: Explain why thick ropes used in cranes are made of a number of thin wires twisted together rather than a single solid wire of the same cross-section.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: The safe load depends on the total cross-sectional area (load $=\text{safe stress}\times A$), which a bundle of thin wires can match.
  2. Step 2: A stranded rope is far more flexible — it bends easily over pulleys and drums without developing dangerous bending stresses, unlike a stiff solid wire.
  3. Step 3: If one strand develops a flaw it can be detected and the rope replaced before all strands fail, improving safety against elastic fatigue.

Answer: Stranded ropes give the same load capacity with much greater flexibility and safety than a single thick wire.

recap: Elastic PE stored in a stretched wire: $U=\frac{1}{2}\times F\times\Delta L=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}\times\text{volume}$.
Elastic energy density (per unit volume): $u=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{(\text{stress})^2}{Y}$, the area under the stress–strain line.
Elastic after-effect is the delay before a body fully recovers; elastic fatigue is the weakening under repeated stress cycles.
Beams sag by $\delta=\frac{W L^3}{4 b d^3 Y}$; since $\delta\propto\frac{1}{d^3}$, beams are made deep and use an I-section.
Ropes use many thin twisted strands for flexibility and a factor of safety; column height is limited by compressive strength.

quiz.q: The elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire is:
quiz.explanation: The force grows from 0 to $F$, so the work stored is $\frac{1}{2}F\,\Delta L=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}\times\text{volume}$.

quiz.q: The elastic energy per unit volume equals:
quiz.explanation: Energy density $u=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}$, the area under the stress–strain line.

quiz.q: The gradual weakening of a material under repeated cycles of stress is called:
quiz.explanation: Elastic fatigue is the loss of strength under repeated loading; the after-effect is merely a delay in recovery.

quiz.q: Girders used in bridges are given an I-shaped cross-section mainly to:
quiz.explanation: An I-section places material where bending stress is largest, giving high stiffness with minimum weight.

online.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids — Online Test

questions.q: Stress is defined as:
options: change in length per unit length
questions.explanation: Stress $=\frac{F}{A}$, the internal restoring force per unit cross-sectional area.

questions.q: The SI unit of stress is:
questions.explanation: Stress is force per unit area, so its unit is $\text{N/m}^2$ (pascal).

questions.q: Strain is:
questions.explanation: Strain is a ratio of like quantities, hence dimensionless with no unit.

questions.q: Hooke's law holds:
questions.explanation: Stress is proportional to strain only within the elastic (proportional) limit.

questions.q: A tangential force applied to a face produces:
questions.explanation: A force parallel to a face slides layers over one another, producing shear (tangential) stress.

questions.q: Young's modulus is given by:
questions.explanation: $Y=\frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}=\frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of stress is:
questions.explanation: Stress $=\frac{\text{force}}{\text{area}}=\frac{[\text{MLT}^{-2}]}{[\text{L}^2]}=[\text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]$.

questions.q: A steel wire of area $1\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$ carries a 50 N load. The tensile stress is:
questions.explanation: Stress $=\frac{50}{1\times10^{-6}}=5\times10^{7}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

questions.q: The bulk modulus is defined as:
questions.explanation: $B=-\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$; the negative sign keeps $B$ positive as volume decreases under pressure.

questions.q: Compressibility is:
questions.explanation: Compressibility $k=\frac{1}{B}$.

questions.q: The shear (rigidity) modulus is possessed by:
questions.explanation: Only solids resist a change of shape; fluids at rest cannot sustain shear stress.

questions.q: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of:
questions.explanation: $\sigma=-\frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}$, a dimensionless number.

questions.q: For most metals Poisson's ratio lies roughly between:
questions.explanation: Typical metals have $\sigma\approx0.2$–$0.4$.

questions.q: The elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire is:
questions.explanation: Average force is $\frac{F}{2}$, so $U=\frac{1}{2}F\Delta L$.

questions.q: The elastic energy stored per unit volume equals:
questions.explanation: Energy density $u=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}$.

questions.q: On the stress–strain curve, the point beyond which a body does not regain its original shape is the:
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation becomes permanent (plastic).

questions.q: The gradual loss of strength of a material under repeated stress cycles is called:
questions.explanation: Elastic fatigue is the weakening that occurs after many loading–unloading cycles.

questions.q: A wire stretches by 2 mm under a force of 200 N. The elastic energy stored is:
questions.explanation: $U=\frac{1}{2}\times200\times2\times10^{-3}=0.2\ \text{J}$.

questions.q: Among steel, copper and rubber, the material with the largest Young's modulus is:
questions.explanation: Steel ($Y\approx2\times10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^2$) is the stiffest of the three.

questions.q: Bridge girders are given an I-section mainly to:
options: give high stiffness with minimum material
questions.explanation: An I-section concentrates material where bending stress is greatest, giving strength with low weight.

imo.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids — IMO / Olympiad Test

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and length have radii in the ratio 1:2. Under the same load, the ratio of their extensions is:
questions.explanation: $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}\propto\frac{1}{r^2}$; with radii $1:2$, extensions are $\frac{1}{1}:\frac{1}{4}=4:1$.

questions.q: A wire of length $L$ and area $A$ has Young's modulus $Y$. If it is cut into two equal halves, the Young's modulus of each half is:
questions.explanation: Young's modulus is a material property; it does not change when the wire is cut.

questions.q: A wire stretches by $\Delta L$ under a load. If both its length and radius are doubled with the same load, the new extension is:
questions.explanation: $\Delta L\propto\frac{L}{r^2}$; new $=\frac{2L}{(2r)^2}=\frac{2L}{4r^2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{L}{r^2}$, so it halves.

questions.q: The work done in stretching a wire by an amount $x$ (extension proportional to force) is proportional to:
questions.explanation: $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ since the restoring force is proportional to $x$, so $U\propto x^2$.

questions.q: If the stress on a wire is doubled (still elastic), the elastic energy stored per unit volume becomes:
questions.explanation: $u=\frac{1}{2}\frac{(\text{stress})^2}{Y}\propto(\text{stress})^2$, so doubling stress quadruples $u$.

questions.q: A material has bulk modulus $B$. The fractional change in volume produced by a pressure $P$ is:
questions.explanation: $B=\frac{P}{\Delta V/V}$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V}=\frac{P}{B}$.

questions.q: For a perfectly incompressible material, the bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio are respectively:
questions.explanation: Incompressible means $\Delta V=0$, so $B\to\infty$ and Poisson's ratio takes its limiting value $0.5$.

questions.q: Two rods of the same material and length, with cross-sectional areas $A$ and $2A$, support the same load. The ratio of elastic energy stored (rod 1 : rod 2) is:
questions.explanation: $U=\frac{F^2 L}{2AY}\propto\frac{1}{A}$; areas $A:2A$ give energies $\frac{1}{A}:\frac{1}{2A}=2:1$.

questions.q: The depression of a beam loaded at its centre varies with its length $L$ as:
questions.explanation: $\delta=\frac{WL^3}{4bd^3Y}\propto L^3$.

questions.q: A load is suspended from a steel and a copper wire of equal length and area in series. The stress in each wire is:
questions.explanation: The same force acts on the same area in each wire, so the stress is identical; only the strains differ.

questions.q: If a wire obeying Hooke's law is stretched to twice its natural length (hypothetically elastic throughout), the energy stored compared with a stretch to 1.5 times its natural length increases by a factor of about:
questions.explanation: Energy $\propto(\text{extension})^2$; extensions are $L$ and $0.5L$, so the ratio is $\frac{(1.0)^2}{(0.5)^2}=4$.

questions.q: A spherical ball of bulk modulus $B$ is taken to a depth where the pressure is $P$. The fractional decrease in its radius is approximately:
questions.explanation: $\frac{\Delta V}{V}=\frac{P}{B}$ and $\frac{\Delta V}{V}=3\frac{\Delta r}{r}$, so $\frac{\Delta r}{r}=\frac{P}{3B}$.
